sections.title: The pursuit of truth
sections.subtitle: Six steps from motivation to belief refinement

tiers.title: Motivation for knowing our purpose and following the truth
tiers.name: Motivation

internals.claim: Without an honest motive to seek truth, all downstream inquiry is corruptible by preference.
internals.soWhat: Locks in the precondition for every later step: the reader has to actually want truth more than comfort.
unlocks: The reader's willingness to entertain conclusions they don't prefer
A baseline against which later steps can be checked for motivated reasoning
eliminates: Inquiries undertaken to confirm an existing belief
Reasoning that bends evidence to fit preferred outcomes
unknown: This step doesn't fix which substantive truths exist — only that the reader is positioned to find them

objections.text: Curiosity can substitute for moral motivation

sections.title: Building confidence in a claim
sections.subtitle: Two parallel claim types supported by seven tiers of confidence-building

internals.claim: A claim's confidence rises when independent sources — lacking motive or contact to collude — agree on its substance.
internals.soWhat: Unlocks tier 4 (chain integrity): without corroboration, transmission integrity has nothing to compare against.
unlocks: Reduces dependence on any single source
eliminates: Single-source claims with no corroboration cannot pass this tier
unknown: Number of corroborators needed scales with claim scope; this tier doesn't fix the threshold

sections.title: Religious comparison: alignment with reality
sections.subtitle: Worldviews ordered along the atheism→monotheism spectrum

criteria.header: 1 · Things are identified by distinguishing their properties from others.

cells.text: 3 Persons distinction neither fundamental nor superficial

criteria.synthesis: Three worldviews pass cleanly; Trinitarianism produces an undecidable distinction that resists identification.

criteria.header: 2 · All information comes from a source.

cells.text: Infinite regress or creation from nothing

criteria.synthesis: Atheism is the only worldview where information has no source — eliminating it at this tier.

criteria.header: 3 · Every inference has a limit; speculation is neither proof nor refutation.
criteria.synthesis: Both eliminated worldviews retreat to speculative exceptions; monotheistic positions absorb the constraint cleanly.

sections.title: Historical reliability of scripture
sections.subtitle: Source-by-source comparison across the worldview spectrum

criteria.header: 1 · Manuscript dating and earliest surviving sources

cells.quote: No sacred manuscript posited; religious texts treated as cultural artifact.
cells.analysis: Disqualified by exclusion — no candidate at this tier.

cells.quote: Vedas preserved orally from ~1500 BCE; Egyptian, Greek, Norse vary widely.
cells.analysis: Strong oral preservation in one tradition; methodology varies elsewhere.

cells.quote: Earliest fragment c. 125 CE — ~90 years after Jesus's death.
cells.analysis: Originals lost; complete codices date to 4th century.
Complete copies within ~20 years of Prophet's death.

criteria.synthesis: Origin-to-manuscript gap: ~20 years (Quran), ~90 years (NT), millennia with oral preservation (Vedas). Shorter gap = stronger historical anchor; oral methodology can partially compensate when rigorous.

criteria.header: 2 · Chain of transmission and textual variants

cells.quote: No text held as preserved; no transmission claim.
cells.analysis: Excluded — no scriptural commitment to evaluate.

cells.quote: Vedas preserved via strict mnemonic chains, mathematically verifiable.
cells.analysis: Comparable rigor for Vedas; most others lack equivalent methodology.

cells.quote: ~5,800 Greek manuscripts; ~400,000 variants — more variants than NT words.
cells.analysis: Successive copying across languages; some variants affect doctrine.

cells.quote: Each verse traceable via named chain, cross-verified within first century.
cells.analysis: Oral and written transmission preserved in parallel; Uthmanic standardization.

criteria.synthesis: Verification mode differs: dual oral+written (Quran), manuscript volume (NT), mnemonic precision (Vedas), n/a (Atheism). Different methodologies produce different forms of confidence — but only some are auditable end-to-end.

sections.title: Theological comparison
sections.subtitle: New Testament vs. Quran, grouped by topic

topics.title: Christology
topics.subtitle: The nature, mission, and return of Jesus across the two traditions

cells.text: Second Person of the Trinity, incarnated as a fully human being while remaining fully God.
Messiah, born of a virgin, sent as a messenger of God — fully human, not divine; Q4:171, Q5:75.

criteria.synthesis: Both affirm Jesus as a singular figure; they diverge on whether divine and human natures can coexist in one person.

cells.text: The crucifixion is the central salvific event; resurrection on the third day vindicates the atonement.
Raised to God before the crucifixion attempt; one was made to appear like him; Q4:157–158.

criteria.synthesis: Christianity treats the crucifixion as the central salvific event; Islam treats it as a historical event divinely interrupted.

topics.synthesis: Across all christological tests, the two traditions diverge on Jesus's ontology, the necessity of his crucifixion, and his eschatological role. The split reduces to one metaphysical commitment: can a divine being become embodied? Christianity says yes and treats the incarnation, death, and resurrection as the central salvific arc; Islam says no and treats Jesus as the highest of the prophets within a strict monotheism. Every downstream christological disagreement traces back to this single yes/no.
